citations.title: Final 2026 Knesset election results as published by Central Elections Committee
citations.excerpt: The Central Elections Committee published the final results of the 2026 national election. Official turnout was 77.9% with 5,716,665 votes cast. Seat distribution: Likud 27, Yashar 21, B’Yachad 12, Joint List 11, Democrats 8, Ra’am 8, Yisrael Beytenu 7, United Torah Judaism 7, Otzma Yehudit 7, Shas 6, Religious Zionism 6. Pro-Netanyahu bloc 53 seats, anti-Netanyahu bloc 48, Arab parties 19. The committee reiterated that investigation into alleged foreign influence will not affect the final results. Reports of widespread voter fraud are entirely unfounded. The elections were conducted lawfully and the integrity of the process was safeguarded.

citations.title: With all votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48, Arab parties 19
citations.excerpt: The Central Elections Committee (CEC) published the final results of the 2026 national election in the early hours of Friday morning. The full official results are slated to be presented to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday, after the CEC completes any final inquiries into errors or complaints. Following that, Herzog will meet with each party leader as they issue their recommendation for the person they believe should form the next government. The final voter turnout was 77.9% of eligible voters — the highest figure in decades — with 5,716,665 votes cast. The final results give Likud 27 seats, Yashar 21, B’Yachad 12, the Joint List 11, The Democrats 8, Ra’am 8, Yisrael Beytenu 7, United Torah Judaism 7, Otzma Yehudit 7, Shas 6 and Religious Zionism 6. Yoaz Hendel’s Reservists-Economic party fell below the 3.25% electoral threshold with 2.63% of the vote, along with Ofer Winter’s People of Israel, which had collected just 1.7% of the vote. These results leave the pro-Netanyahu bloc with 53 seats, the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 48 and the Arab factions with 19. The parties in the pro-Netanyahu bloc, which comprise the current government, held 68 seats in the outgoing Knesset, marking a significant drop. The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and Ra’am — won an all-time high of 19 seats, an all-time high and almost double their current 10 seats. This would be more than enough to tip the anti-Netanyahu bloc into a comfortable majority, if all Zionist bloc members except The Democrats hadn’t ruled out cooperating with Ra’am or the Joint List. In its statement early Friday morning, the CEC reiterated comments made by acting director Dean Livne earlier Thursday, rejecting claims of widespread voter fraud amid reports of a possible Qatari campaign to influence the vote. “Reports published throughout the day are entirely unfounded,” Livne said, noting that the investigation “will not affect the final results submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population.”

citations.title: Election committee chief instructs Shin Bet to probe suspicion of foreign influence on vote
citations.excerpt: In a political bombshell, it was revealed Thursday that Central Elections Committee chair Justice Noam Sohlberg has asked the Shin Bet to investigate “serious suspicions” of foreign interference in Tuesday’s election, with Hebrew media reporting suspicions that Qatar had sent significant funds to Israel to influence the Arab vote. “Serious suspicions have been brought to my attention regarding improper influence on the elections — exerted through funding provided by foreign entities acting against Israeli interests,” Sohlberg wrote in a letter to Zini dated Wednesday. “While I cannot attest to the substance of these suspicions, it is my view that — given they involve foreign entities — there is an obligation to investigate them thoroughly,” he said. Several outlets, including Channel 12 and Ynet, reported that the information was given to Sohlberg by the Shin Bet. “This is an investigation opened in the past two weeks based on solid intelligence information,” an unnamed security official told Kan news. Near-final election results on Thursday showed the bloc supporting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu winning 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, with the Zionist opposition at 48, and Arab parties at an unprecedented 19. The revelation of Sohlberg’s letter led to immediate allegations by coalition parties that the election had been “stolen.” Opposition leaders called for a thorough investigation, but warned against any political attempt to use the claim to illegitimately influence the election results, so long as the suspicions have not been substantiated. Acting CEC director general Dean Livne rejected on Thursday afternoon allegations of widespread voter fraud as baseless, reiterating that the vote was conducted lawfully and that to the best of the committee’s knowledge, there was no evidence of systematic irregularities. “The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity,” Livne wrote.

citations.title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
citations.excerpt: The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority. Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey. Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha. Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament. The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters. That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48. On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims. Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government. But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."

citations.title: Israel’s anti-Qatar campaign bleeds into elections
citations.excerpt: As Israel awaits the final results of its highly contested elections , some political figures have sought to drag Qatar into the fray with claims of voting interference – an accusation Doha rejects. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and media outlets associated with it have, without evidence, accused Qatar of sending money to Arab parties in Israel for get-out-the-vote drives. Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman on Thursday categorically denied the allegations of interference or funding of any activities aimed at influencing the election results. “We reject the accusations made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes following this week’s elections,” Majed al-Ansari said in a post on X. Despite the latest claims, Dean Livine, the acting director for Israel’s Central Elections Committee, has rejected allegations of foreign interference in the elections. “The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded,” he wrote in a letter to an MP and fellow committee member. He reiterated that Qatar has “no involvement” in Israel’s political or electoral competition. “These are internal Israeli matters in which we do not interfere, and we will not accept any attempt to draw Qatar into its domestic political disputes.”

passages.text: Israel’s 2026 Knesset election produced a hung parliament. After the complete count, including double-envelope ballots, the pro-Netanyahu bloc secured 53 seats, the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot 48 seats, and the two Arab lists a combined record 19 seats. Turnout reached 77.9 percent.

Central Elections Committee chair Justice Noam Sohlberg asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions of foreign funding aimed at influencing the vote, widely reported as possible Qatari support for Arab get-out-the-vote efforts. Coalition figures labeled the situation “Ra’amgate” and claimed the election was stolen.

Acting CEC director Dean Livne publicly rejected claims of systematic fraud or interference that would affect results, stating the elections were conducted lawfully and the probe will not change the numbers presented to the president.

The Central Elections Committee has confirmed the final seat totals and stated that ongoing inquiries into possible foreign influence do not alter the published results or the integrity of the polling process.

Qatar’s Foreign Ministry categorically denied any interference or funding of activities intended to influence the Israeli election, calling the allegations a disinformation campaign. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of attempting to delegitimise the results.

President Herzog will receive official results and begin consultations. Coalition arithmetic remains blocked without Arab parties, which most Zionist parties have ruled out. The Shin Bet probe’s findings, due within a week, will shape the political narrative around legitimacy.
